stories.headline: Athletic finds Russini-Vrabel ties violated newsroom standards
stories.summary: Former Athletic reporter Dianna Russini's relationship with Mike Vrabel violated newsroom standards but showed no clear bias toward the Patriots head coach, the Athletic said Thursday.
stories.body:
Former Athletic reporter Dianna Russini's relationship with Mike Vrabel violated newsroom standards but showed no clear bias toward the New England Patriots head coach, according to the findings of an internal investigation into her work published on the company's website Thursday.

"Russini's relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic's standards," Mike Semel, the outlet's editorial director for standards and editorial quality, wrote in the report. "Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed."

As for Russini's coverage of Vrabel, Semel wrote: "I've not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to help promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic. That said, there are examples of Russini writing glowingly of Vrabel that in hindsight are awkward or even uncomfortable."

The findings are the result of a nearly five-month investigation that began after the New York Post published photographs of Russini with Vrabel together at an adults-only resort, shortly after which Russini resigned from the New York Times-owned Athletic.

The Athletic and New York Times declined to comment beyond the public report. Russini declined to comment.

According to the report, Semel reviewed 903 stories and 77 videos that contained Russini's byline, contributor line or a mention of her reporting. He analyzed 204 episodes of a podcast Russini co-hosted and a number of appearances she made on other outlets while representing the Athletic. He interviewed Athletic staff, as well, though he did not speak to Russini, according to a source with direct knowledge of the investigation.

The person said the Athletic had no access to Russini's phone and that the report was solely focused on her publicly available reporting. The Athletic began an inquiry into Russini's relationship with Vrabel while she was an employee, but ended it once she resigned. The report stated that the Athletic did not complete an investigation or reach a conclusion about the nature of Russini's relationship with Vrabel.

"The vast majority of Russini's work for The Athletic had nothing to do with Vrabel, the teams he was coaching or the players the team was pursuing," Semel wrote. "In interviews with editors and reporters with whom she worked most closely, it was clear Russini was sourced up around the NFL, not just with Vrabel or the Patriots."

Still, Semel wrote, "the appearances surrounding her relationship with Vrabel undermines our audience's confidence in her impartiality."

Semel suggested adding editor's notes to two pieces of Athletic content following the review. The first is a "lighthearted" video in which Russini referred to Vrabel as "somewhat heroic" for his role in breaking up a training camp fight. The second instance is a column in which information was not properly attributed, according to the report.

Semel reported that he found no inaccuracies in Russini's reporting, though it identified one piece from 2023 in which Russini reported Vrabel's coaching job in Tennessee was safe less than two months before he was ultimately fired. "No other media came out as strongly about Vrabel's job security," the report said, though it added it was difficult to prove Russini hadn't spoken to Titans sources and that the story wasn't accurate at the time of publication.

In Russini's resignation letter, she wrote, "I have covered the NFL with professionalism and dedication throughout my career, and I stand behind every story I have ever published."

The Athletic's executive editor Steven Ginsberg initially issued a public defense of Russini after the Post published the photos and said the matter had been taken out of context. Later, he wrote a memo to Athletic staff saying, "As additional information emerged, new questions were raised that became part of our investigation."

The report concluded with recommendations that the Athletic should add a meeting with the standards editor as part of its onboarding process for new hires and that the company must be vigilant in enforcing its conflict of interest guidelines and sourcing standards, including asking reporters to disclose anonymous sources to their editors.

stories.headline: Premier League sets new record for transfer spending
stories.summary: The Premier League set a new record for transfer spending as the window closed with a flurry of deals.
stories.body:
The Premier League set a new record for transfer spending as the window closed with a flurry of deals.

More than half of the top flight's clubs broke their transfer records in a summer window featuring four of the most expensive ever signings.

The final two days of the window pushed summer spending significantly beyond last season's record of £3.14 billion ($4.23bn) with confirmed figures exceeding £3.3b ($4.4bn).

First Liverpool spent an initial £106 million ($144m) potentially rising to £123m ($165m) on Paris Saint-Germain winger Bradley Barcola, then City paired Elliot Anderson with another nine-figure midfielder in former Chelsea star Enzo Fernández -- whose £125m ($168m) move matched the British record set 12 months ago by Barcola's new teammate Alexander Isak.

Earlier in the summer, England internationals Anderson and Morgan Rogers joined Manchester City for £116m ($156m) and Chelsea for £117m ($157m) respectively.

Sandro Tonali's move from Newcastle to Tottenham has the potential to become a fifth £100m-plus ($134.8m-plus) deal this summer, with the initial £92.5m ($124.6m) marking the second time Spurs had broken their club record as it came hot on the heels of Mateus Fernandes' £85m ($114.5m) arrival from West Ham.

Savio's £75m ($101m) switch from City slotted in third on Spurs' all-time list, with manager Roberto De Zerbi admitting "the transfer market is crazy" -- reflecting a league-wide summer of spending.

Eleven clubs in all have broken their transfer records, six of them on more than one occasion.

Coventry have done so four times over, signing Aurèle Amenda for an initial £15.4m ($20.7m) before Loum Tchaouna became their first ever £20m ($26m) signing, Carl Rushworth made his loan move permanent for a £22.5m ($30.3m) fee and Caleb Yirenkyi nudged the record up to £23.1m ($31m.)

Three clubs broke their transfer records to sign goalkeepers, with James Trafford costing Leeds £40m ($53.9m) while, like Rushworth, Konstantinos Tsolakis' move to Hull was overtaken by Nobel Mendy's £22m ($29.6m) arrival.

Aston Villa and Ipswich are the other clubs to break their respective records twice while Mamadou Sangare (Brentford), Luka Vuskovic (Brighton) and Liam Delap (Nottingham Forest) were all £40m-plus ($53.9m-plus) club-record buys.

- Man City sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea for joint-record fee

- Premier League transfers: Under-the-radar deals you missed - but need to know about

- Chelsea, Real Madrid win transfer window; Liverpool biggest losers

There have been nine moves worth an initial £75m ($101m) or more -- a list completed by City and Arsenal midfielders Ayyoub Bouaddi and Bruno Guimarães -- plus £65m ($87m) moves for Carlos Baleba to Manchester United and Nicolas Jackson to Aston Villa.

On the other side of the balance sheet, Newcastle raised over £235m ($316m) from the three sales of Tonali, Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon while Villa banked £50m-plus ($67m-plus) fees for Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins in addition to Rogers' Chelsea.

It was also a record-breaking transfer window worldwide, seeing an increase in the amount of money spent and a greater number of moves than last year.

Fees topped than more £7.24bn ($9.8bn), up more than 1.5% on 12 months ago, with the number of transfers rising by 6% to 12,575, setting a new mark for the mid-year window.

According to figures released in FIFA's International Transfer Snapshot, English clubs led global spending, with more than £2.2bn ($3bn) invested in transfer fees, ahead of Italy (£810million), Spain (£695m), Germany (£668m) and France (£474m).

stories.headline: 2026 NBA buzz: Latest free agency and trade updates
stories.summary: We're tracking deals, trades and buzz across the NBA, including the latest on Kawhi Leonard and the NBA's investigation into the Clippers.
stories.body:
NBA free agency has almost reached the end, with several players landing in new homes this offseason.

LeBron James decided to continue his historic career with the Philadelphia 76ers after months of deliberation. The Sixers also traded for Jaylen Brown this summer, turning the franchise into a true contender with two huge moves.

Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo is headed to South Beach to team up with Bam Adebayo and the Miami Heat, and the Los Angeles Lakers have been sold for the second time in 10 months.

What will happen next during this turbulent offseason?

Check back here for all the latest buzz, news and reactions from our ESPN NBA insiders, with the latest info at the top:

Quick links:

Free agency grades | Trade grades

Trade tracker | Transactions

Depth charts | Trade machine | More

Sept. 3

Windhorst: Steve Ballmer 'very' angry after NBA penalty
ESPN's Brian Windhorst reported that LA Clippers owner Steve Ballmer is 'very angry' after the penalties handed down to the franchise by the NBA on Sept. 2.

"When you're worth $150 billion and you're angry, and he's very clearly angry, you can't advise him, you can't talk to him," Windhorst said on Get Up. "I'd be stunned if his lawyers didn't advise him, as Shams [Charania] said, to make a plea deal because he should've made a please deal."

Read more: NBA punishes Clippers after Kawhi investigation: Top questions​

Thompson, Rockets agree to five-year contract extension

The Houston Rockets and Amen Thompson have agreed to a five-year, $208 million rookie-scale contract extension, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania The deal includes a 10% trade kicker.

Sept. 2

NBA insiders answer the biggest questions on NBA's Clippers investigation
After the NBA released the findings of its yearlong investigation into allegations that the LA Clippers circumvented the salary cap in order to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard, ESPN NBA insiders Baxter Holmes, Brian Windhorst, Ramona Shelburne and Bobby Marks examined the report, the massive punishments the NBA leveled and how all of it could impact this season -- and beyond.

The punishment was compounded by the Clippers being previous offenders during Steve Ballmer's tenure as owner. They were fined $250,000 for a similar accusation involving DeAndre Jordan in 2015. There also was a 2019 investigation into Leonard's signing in which the Clippers were cleared of wrongdoing but subsequently warned and put through a seminar to remind them of the rules.
This penalty is indeed harsh, but it could have been worse.

In the case of Joe Smith and the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2000, his contract was voided and his Bird rights were vacated.

Leonard will have to write a sizable check -- $700,000 -- but he will not be suspended, and his contract and Bird rights remain unaffected.

The Clippers and the Toronto Raptors will be allowed to move forward in their trade process, one league source said. If the trade moves forward, LA will acquire two first-round picks in the deal. -- Windhorst

Read the full story here.

Charania: NBA rules on Kawhi Leonard-Aspiration investigation

Sources told ESPN's Shams Charania reported that, after a year-long probe into Kawhi Leonard-Aspiration connection, the NBA has stripped the LA Clippers of five first-round picks and issued a $30 million fine to owner Steve Ballmer, as well as suspended Ballmer, Lawrence Frank and Gillian Zucker.

On top of that, Leonard will have to pay $700,000 in restitution for improper benefits by the franchise for his uncle and former business representative, Dennis Robertson. Leonard will not be suspended but Robertson is banned by the NBA from all business dealings.

SEC requesting information from Daktronics regarding Clippers probe
The Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking information from Daktronics, the company that designed the LA Clippers' videoboard inside the Intuit Dome, related to Kawhi Leonard, a company executive said Wednesday.

"Let me now briefly address a matter that has been in the media concerning the NBA's investigation of Kawhi Leonard and the Clippers in connection with the league's collective bargaining agreement that many of you may have heard about," chief financial officer Howard Atkins said on Daktronics' quarterly earnings call.

"As you might expect, we have received requests for information from the NBA. Additionally, the Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking information from us concerning the company and Mr. Leonard. "We take these requests seriously and are cooperating. At this point, out of respect for the respective processes, we will not be providing further comment."

A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment.

Podcaster Pablo Torre reported last month that Daktronics had an undisclosed sponsorship agreement allegedly worth millions of dollars with Leonard.

Torre interviewed someone identified as an "anonymous high-level source under contract for Intuit Dome" who alleged that the sponsorship deal "was 1,000% a way to circumvent the salary cap. It was funneling money from the Clippers through Daktronics back to Kawhi."

The NBA launched its investigation into the Clippers and Leonard last September after numerous podcasts from Torre, who cited internal documents that showed that Clippers owner Steve Ballmer invested $50 million in Aspiration, a now-defunct green banking company, through his personal LLC in September 2021.

That month, the Clippers signed a 23-year, $300 million deal with Aspiration, making the company the "first founding partner" of the Intuit Dome.

Six months later, Aspiration signed its $28 million endorsement deal with Leonard.

An unnamed employee who purportedly worked for the banking company told Torre that Leonard's sponsorship deal "was to circumvent the salary cap."

The Clippers have repeatedly denied that they funneled money through Aspiration to compensate Leonard.

On Aug. 17, ESPN reported that the NBA has found no evidence showing Ballmer funneled money through team sponsors to pay Leonard in order to circumvent the salary cap, per three people with knowledge of recent discussions between the two sides. -- Baxter Holmes

Sept. 1

Windhorst: Sabonis hired new agent this summer, could want out of Sacramento

On the Sept. 1 episode of "The Hoop Collective," ESPN's Brian Windhorst discussed what Domantas Sabonis hiring a new agent this summer could mean for his future with the Sacramento Kings.

Windhorst on Sabonis hiring a new agent: " I do think it's somewhat interesting that he changed agents this offseason. He hired Aaron Mintz of CAA. Steve Heumann and that group. One of the top executives at CAA. This last year, Mintz and his group executed the trade for Trae Young away from Atlanta, executed the trade for Walker Kessler away from the [Jazz]. Domantas Sabonis just hired him.

"At the risk of ... parodying myself from the season, why would he do that?"

Aug. 29

Latest on Curry's next deal decision

The window for Stephen Curry to sign an extension has officially opened.

The four-time champion and two-time MVP is now eligible (through June 30) to sign a two-year, $136.7 million extension. If he signs, Curry will become the first player in NBA history to rack up more than $600 million in on-court earnings.

A new contract for Curry will have important financial implications for Golden State. With Curry, Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III able to become free agents after the 2026-27 season, Golden State could have significant cap space to reshape its roster.

If Curry signs for the maximum allowed in the first season of an extension ($65.7 million), the Warriors project to have between $45 million and $60 million in cap space next offseason. -- Bobby Marks

Wolves, Jazz swap forwards
The Minnesota Timberwolves are trading forward Josh Green to the Utah Jazz for forwards Cody Williams and John Konchar, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

The Wolves are expected to keep Williams, the No. 10 pick in 2024, and waive-and-stretch Konchar, sources said. By moving Green's $14.7 million salary, Minnesota can sign Jonathan Kuminga to the taxpayer midlevel exception.

Aug. 27

Free agent center Richards agrees to one-year deal with Heat
Free agent center Nick Richards has agreed to a one-year deal with the Miami Heat, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. After signing Klay Thompson, the Heat fill roster slot No. 14 with a reserve big man.

Aug. 26

Kuminga signs two-year deal with Minnesota
Free agent forward Jonathan Kuminga agreed to a two-year, $12.4 million deal with the Minnesota Timberwolves, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Kuminga probably will start alongside Anthony Edwards, LaMelo Ball, Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert.

Mathurin to sign with Pels
Free agent guard Bennedict Mathurin agreed to a two-year, $16 million deal with the New Orleans Pelicans, including a player option, sources tell ESPN.

Aug. 25

Warriors agree to deal with Niang

Forward Georges Niang agreed to a one-year, $3.9 million deal with the Golden State Warriors, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Warriors sign guard Williams
Free agent guard Brandon Williams is signing a one-year, $2.6M deal with the Golden State Warriors, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Williams averaged 13 points and 3.9 assists per game last season for the Dallas Mavericks.

Aug. 24

Blazers lose Sharpe to injury
Portland Trail Blazers guard Shaedon Sharpe sustained a torn meniscus in his right knee, and he is expected to miss six months, sources told ESPN.

Sharpe, 23, averaged 20.8 points for the Blazers last season but missed a large chunk of the campaign with a stress fracture of his left fibula.

His four-year, $90 million extension, which he signed last year, officially kicks in this season. Sharpe will make $20.1 million in 2026-27.

Aug. 21

Nuggets signing DeRozan to one-year deal
Six-time NBA All-Star DeMar DeRozan agreed to sign with the Denver Nuggets on a one-year, $3.9 million deal, sources told ESPN on Friday.

DeRozan landed on the Nuggets after speaking to the Miami Heat, Washington Wizards and New Orleans Pelicans during free agency, choosing a significant role in Denver and a chance to compete in the West. The Nuggets' front office and coaches made a strong recruitment effort in recent weeks to secure DeRozan's commitment, showing him how he would complement Nikola Jokic and Jamal Murray as an additional playmaker. He also gives the Nuggets a veteran backcourt presence after sending young, versatile wing Peyton Watson to Cleveland as part of a four-team trade.

Mavs buy out Thompson, to sign with Heat
Klay Thompson is expected to sign with the Miami Heat after clearing waivers following his contract buyout from the Dallas Mavericks, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Friday.

Thompson, 36, was due to make $17.5 million in the final season of his contract with the Mavericks, who announced his buyout Friday afternoon.

He played two seasons for the Mavericks, averaging 12.9 points per game and shooting 38.7% from 3-point range. Thompson passed Damian Lillard last season to rank fourth in career 3-pointers made.

Aug. 20

Harden to return to Cavs
Free agent James Harden agreed to sign a three-year, $97M contract to return to the Cleveland Cavaliers, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania, with a player option for the 2028-29 season.

The Cavs acquired Harden, who turns 37 on Aug. 26, from the LA Clippers in early February in a trade for guard Darius Garland. Cleveland went 21-9 after Harden debuted, tied for the fifth-best record after Feb. 7, as he averaged 20.5 points, 7.7 assists and 4.8 rebounds per game after the All-Star break.

Aug. 19

Watson to Cavs in multiteam trade
The Cleveland Cavaliers, Denver Nuggets and LA Clippers agreed on a trade sending Peyton Watson to the Cavaliers, Max Strus to LA, and an unprotected 2031 Cavs first-round pick and 2032 Sacramento Kings second-rounder to the Nuggets, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. As part of the trade, the Cavaliers will send Tre Mann to the Washington Wizards for Cam Whitmore and a 2027 second-round pick.

Watson will sign a new four-year, $88 million deal with Cleveland.

Aug. 17

Suns, Highsmith agree to one-year deal

The Phoenix Suns and forward Haywood Highsmith agreed to a one-year deal, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Watford, Pelicans agree to one-year deal
Free agent forward Trendon Watford agreed to a one-year, $2.9 million deal with the New Orleans Pelicans, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Watford, 25, considered multiple options, but for New Orleans he serves as a productive two-way get late into the offseason.

Aug. 14

Cavaliers trade Schroder, cash to Hornets for Mann
The Cleveland Cavaliers are trading Dennis Schroder and cash to the Charlotte Hornets for Tre Mann, sources told ESPN on Friday.

The Hornets, Cavaliers and Schroder's rep, Mark Bartelstein of Priority Sports, worked for the past couple months on the deal, which also provides Cleveland flexibility to continue pursuing roster moves and tax savings to keep the team well under the second apron, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

Aug. 13

Beal re-signs with Clippers
Free agent guard Bradley Beal agreed to a two-year, $13.2 million deal to return to the LA Clippers, with a player option in the second season, Mark Bartelstein of Priority Sports told ESPN.

After declining his $5.6 million player option, Beal sifted through options over the last month in free agency, including interest from the Miami Heat, before landing on the Clippers. He returns to LA after rehabbing from hip surgery that cost him all but six games last season.

Aug. 12
Westbrook announces retirement from NBA
Russell Westbrook, the 2017 MVP, a nine-time All-NBA selection and the league's all-time triple-double leader, is retiring from the NBA, the 37-year-old announced on Wednesday. Westbrook had contract offers this offseason from the Sacramento Kings and Washington Wizards but chose to step away on his own terms, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Drafted No. 4 overall by the Seattle SuperSonics in 2008 just before the franchise relocated to Oklahoma City, Westbrook played 11 of his 18 seasons with the Thunder. The electric guard and Hall of Fame lock then spent the remainder of his career with the Houston Rockets, Wizards, Los Angeles Lakers, LA Clippers, Denver Nuggets and Kings.

Westbrook retires with the fifth most assists in NBA history (10,351).

NBA world praises 'legendary' career

Aug. 11

McMenamin: NBA excited to grow product with 3 p.m. opening day tip-off
ESPN's Dave McMenamin went on NBA Today to discuss the recent schedule release for the NBA's opening day and Christmas games.

"I've talked to people around the league today and they're like we could sense the excitement for the NBA right now. So let's experiment with this thing," McMenamin said. "They talked with executives at NBC, and it was kind of a joint decision that this is something we can turn into a celebration of the game. It's already a marquee moment for the league. Let's see if we can enhance it and turn it into a major showcase. Maybe down the line, this becomes a tradition for NBA fans. ... [Also the NBA is] an international game. 3 p.m. Eastern is primetime viewing in Europe."

The Boston Celtics and Detroit Pistons open the season on Tuesday, Oct. 20 at 3 p.m. ET on NBA/Peacock.

What's latest on Kawhi and the Clippers? And updates on Nuggets, Suns
Brian is joined by ESPN's Anthony Slater to discuss the latest in the ongoing Kawhi Leonard-LA Clippers situation, including how it could impact the Toronto Raptors and the Eastern Conference during the 2026-27 season. They move on to the cover the Dillon Brooks' contract and how it impacts the future spending plans for the Phoenix Suns. The duo then closes on how the Denver Nuggets' books put them in trouble moving forward, and a remembrance of Don Nelson.

Windhorst on the newest Kawhi Leonard situation: "That's obviously key: Did he get money from Daktronics? Slater, if this is accurate, the Clippers side of it is devastating.
But let's put that aside for right now. For the actual business of the NBA for the 26-27 season, this is not just a Clipper issue. Last year was a Clipper issue. Now, it is no longer just a Clipper issue. Whether Kahwi Leonard is on the Raptors or not has a huge circumstantial fallout in the Eastern Conference and then obviously like you know DeMar DeRozan is held up to a certain extent, for example. James Harden is hasn't done his business with the Cavs because they're waiting on things.

Latest episodes of the 'Hoop Collective' podcast

Aug. 7

NBA insiders: Updates on the biggest remaining NBA free agents

ESPN's NBA insiders came together to give updates on the top remaining free agents this season. Highlights include:

Multiple teams are pursuing Peyton Watson, including the Atlanta Hawks, LA Clippers, Milwaukee Bucks and Cleveland Cavaliers
The Detroit Pistons remain the favorite to sign Jalen Duren but the two sides are at an impasse
The Los Angeles Lakers are interested Jonathan Kuminga
James Harden is on track for a multi-year deal with Cleveland
DeMar DeRozan has drawn interest from the Miami Heat, Denver Nuggets, Washington Wizards and Cavaliers

Read more: Updates on the biggest remaining NBA free agents

Aug. 5

Brooks, Suns agree to three-year, $73 million extension
Phoenix Suns forward Dillon Brooks agreed Wednesday to a three-year, $73 million contract extension through 2029-30, agent Mike George of Klutch Sports told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Credited with helping to establish a new culture in Phoenix, Brooks is coming off the best season of his nine-year career. He averaged a career-high 20.2 points to go with 3.6 rebounds and 1.8 assists for a surprise 45-win playoff team that maintained continuity throughout the offseason. In addition to bringing back Brooks, the Suns signed Collin Gillespie, Mark Williams and Jordan Goodwin to multiyear contracts and also acquired Miles Bridges and Luke Kennard.

Slater: Kings were actively shopping Sabonis at deadline, draft
ESPN's Anthony Slater reported that the Sacramento Kings were openly shopping forward Domantas Sabonis at the trade deadline and the 2026 draft.

The Kings nearly traded Sabonis to the Toronto Raptors at the deadline in February -- a move he would've welcomed, a source with knowledge of the situation said -- for a package that included RJ Barrett, but the Raptors were unable to get off the three-year, $84 million remaining on Jakob Poeltl's contract, which doomed the deal.
Sabonis had season-ending surgery on a partially torn meniscus later that month, and the Kings revisited trade talks surrounding him this summer. Perry visited with restricted free agent center Jalen Duren in early July and explored the idea of a sign-and-trade swap of big men, but the Detroit Pistons balked at the idea of losing Duren for Sabonis, league sources said.

There were predraft conversations about Sabonis with the Charlotte Hornets (who held pick Nos. 14 and 18) and at least one phone call with the Boston Celtics, team and league sources said, but nothing materialized. In Charlotte's case, the idea would've been to pair Sabonis with point guard LaMelo Ball, but the franchise instead opted to trade Ball for draft picks and lean further into a youth movement.

Read more: Darius Acuff is the Kings' future, but they still have to manage the present

July 30

Shelburne: The Cavaliers are still poking around with Peyton Watson
Appearing on ESPN's "NBA Today," Ramona Shelburne gave the latest on James Harden's free agency status after the All-Star declined a $42.3 million player option. "The Cavs are still poking around with Peyton Watson and I think that's why James has given them a lot of room to negotiate."

Shelburne: The Raptors have given zero indication of backing out of the Leonard trade
Ramona Shelburne appeared on ESPN's "NBA Today" to weigh in on the pending Aspiration investigation after Baxter Holmes reported today that the case could drag into 2027. "I haven't heard [the Raptors] trying to back out. I think the discussion is more of a leaguewide discussion."

July 28

76ers trade Broome, pick to Clippers for cash considerations
The Philadelphia 76ers are trading Johni Broome and a second-round pick to the LA Clippers for cash considerations, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Shams: Nuggets tweak asking price for potential Watson trade

Appearing on ESPN's "NBA Today," Shams Charania reported that the Denver Nuggets have lowered their asking price in a potential sign-and-trade of restricted free agent wing Peyton Watson. "The Nuggets initially had set a price this offseason of -- similar to the Walker Kessler deal -- two firsts and two swaps," Charania said. "Now that price is a really good high-level player as well as a first-round pick."

Shams: Wizards looking to add another scorer?

Appearing on ESPN's "NBA Today," Shams Charania reported that the Washington Wizards have had conversations with free agent guard DeMar DeRozan in recent days. The Wizards join the Miami Heat, Denver Nuggets and Cleveland Cavaliers among franchises to show interest in the six-time All-Star. DeRozan, who will turn 37 in August, was waived by the Sacramento Kings on July 6.

Warriors, Green agree to one-year deal

Draymond Green has agreed to return to the Golden State Warriors on a one-year, $27.7 million deal, Klutch Sports CEO Rich Paul told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Green turned down his $27.6 million player option earlier this summer in a surprising move shortly before free agency kicked off. The decision created financial flexibility for Golden State, which was among the teams in the running to land LeBron James.

However, after James eventually decided to take his talents to Philadelphia, Green and the Warriors moved forward on a new deal.

Will Towns get the max from Knicks?

Appearing on ESPN's "First Take," Brian Windhorst explained why the New York Knicks might hesitate on giving Karl-Anthony Towns a maximum contract extension of four years at $272 million.

"He's extension-eligible now. They could do this deal today. They haven't done the deal. They don't have an agreement on it. KAT is coming off the highest achievement of his career. He was awesome in the playoffs. He could look at the Knicks with a straight face and say 'I'm a max player. Pay me.' But in the modern era, you just have to be careful with this situation. ... Karl Towns absolutely earned and deserves a full max contract. If the Knicks give it to him, I'm not sure they're going to be able to keep this team together multiple years into the future."

Windhorst said that Knicks players such as Jalen Brunson and Mikal Bridges set the precedent of taking less money to help build out the roster, and New York might want Towns to do the same.

July 24

Shams: Inside Philly's recruitment of LeBron

Appearing on ESPN's "SportsCenter," Shams Charania detailed the discussions between the Philadelphia 76ers and LeBron James heading into the superstar's decision. "James was recruited by Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid -- he spoke to both of them. Jaylen Brown actually spoke to his agent, Rich Paul, during the process. And the only coach that LeBron James spoke to during this three-week-long process was Sixers head coach Nick Nurse."

Shelburne details conversation with Rich Paul

Appearing on ESPN's "NBA Today," Ramona Shelburne discussed what Klutch Sports CEO Rich Paul told her Friday afternoon about LeBron James choosing the Philadelphia 76ers over a reunion with the Miami Heat or Cleveland Cavaliers. "When you've been to a place before, when you've won in a place before, if you go back, it may not be the same. You kind of want to leave those memories where they were."

NBA free agent frenzy 2.0 incoming?

With LeBron James joining the Philadelphia 76ers, expect free agency to pick up.

Teams in discussion for James -- Cleveland, Denver, Golden State and Minnesota -- have roster spots to fill and key free agents to sign, notably James Harden, Draymond Green and Peyton Watson. Harden in Cleveland and Green in Golden State will play a role in how much financial flexibility each team has to offer available free agents.

The Cavaliers could have the $6.1 million taxpayer midlevel exception available, but only if Harden's next deal starts between $26 million and $28 million. Otherwise, the veteran minimum exception is the lone signing tool available to fill their two roster spots.
Golden State agreed to sign De'Anthony Melton to a two-year, $11.2 million contract early in free agency. The Warriors are hard-capped at the second apron and will likely have just the veteran minimum exception available after Green signs. They have three open roster spots.
The Nuggets, meanwhile, are in a holding pattern as it relates to restricted free agents Watson and Spencer Jones. Denver not only is a luxury tax team but will become the only team over the second apron if both players re-sign.
The Pistons, at least for now, do not have apron concerns as it relates to restricted free agent Jalen Duren. Detroit is $46 million below the luxury tax and $55 million under the first apron. Why Dolan is so worried about the second apron
The New York Knicks' championship parade has not even started, but there are already questions over whether finances will break up the roster.

"If we could bring back the whole team, exactly as is, why wouldn't you?" Knicks owner James Dolan said Wednesday on WFAN's "Carton Show." "I don't know if we'll be able to.

"We're willing to stretch, but there's certain things in the NBA that you'd have to be suicidal to do. One of them is the second apron. Cannot go into the second apron."

Including the 24th pick in next week's draft (June 23 and 24, 8 p.m. ET on ABC/ESPN), New York is $13 million below the second apron and has decisions with free agents Landry Shamet, Mitchell Robinson and possibly Jose Alvarado. (Alvarado has until Monday to decide on his $4.5 million option.) The entire starting five, meanwhile, is under contract through at least 2026-27. Karl-Anthony Towns is extension-eligible this summer and can become a free agent in the 2027 offseason if an agreement is not reached.

The second apron is a punitive luxury tax threshold restricting how teams add to their rosters in free agency, trades and the draft. In the case of the Knicks, the team would not be allowed to send cash in a trade, use the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception, aggregate salaries in a trade or use more than 100% of the traded player exception.

A team cannot trade its first-round pick seven years out if it finishes over the second apron in consecutive seasons, which no team has ever done. That same pick could be moved back to the end of the first round if a team finishes over the second apron in three out of four seasons. Luckily for Dolan and the Knicks, there are no rules that prohibit a team from retaining its own players.

New York can exceed the threshold to sign Robinson, Shamet and Alvarado. If the Knicks let the three players sign elsewhere, they would have their first-round pick (New York also has the 31st and 55th picks in the second round), the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception and $2.5 million veteran minimum exceptions available as replacements.

Since the apron rules were implemented before the 2024-25 season, Cleveland, Phoenix, Minnesota and Boston have finished the regular season over the second apron. The Knicks finished the past two seasons $53,000 and $370,000 below. Next offseason, New York is projected to be $31 million below the second apron with seven players under contract. -- Bobby Marks

The Minnesota Timberwolves won the battle on Saturday night, with a stirring Game 4 victory over Denver that brought the team within a win of the second round.

But they might have lost the war.

On Saturday night, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Donte DiVincenzo had torn his right Achilles and would miss the rest of the postseason. And on Sunday morning, he reported that four-time All-Star Anthony Edwards would miss multiple weeks after hyperextending his left knee.

Losing a starting backcourt in one fell swoop would hurt any team in the playoffs, but it should be especially tough on Minnesota. The Timberwolves rely on a strong core, with little depth behind it; entering Saturday's games, only seven Wolves had averaged more than 10 minutes per game in the playoffs. By comparison, 10 members for both the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs played more than that, and even the injury-riddled Lakers had eight.

With Edwards and DiVincenzo out, Minnesota's entire rotation and offensive gameplan will shift. Ayo Dosunmu -- fresh off a 43-point outburst -- and Bones Hyland are the likely replacement starters, with some combination of Mike Conley, Terrence Shannon Jr. (who received his first playoff minutes in Game 4) and Kyle Anderson receiving more minutes off the bench.

That might not be a tenable arrangement on offense, unless Dosunmu can continue posting career highs in points going forward. There's very little shooting and playmaking talent left in Minnesota's lineup, and Julius Randle -- who has been only OK against Denver, averaging 17.5 points and 3.5 assists per game on subpar efficiency -- will need to step up in Edwards' stead.

But all isn't lost for the Timberwolves, at least against the Nuggets. Surprisingly, lineups without DiVincenzo and Edwards held their own in the regular season, with a plus-3.0 net rating, per Cleaning the Glass (which removes garbage time). Those groups excelled on defense. And as long as Rudy Gobert and Jaden McDaniels remain on the floor, Minnesota will retain its top two options to guard Nikola Jokic and Jamal Murray, respectively.

Why LaMelo's flagrant 2 falls into a gray area
The NBA retroactively assessed Charlotte Hornets guard LaMelo Ball with a flagrant foul 2 for tripping Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo in Tuesday's Eastern Conference play-in game, which Charlotte won in overtime thanks to Ball's last-second layup.

But for the Heat and their fans, it doesn't erase Adebayo's injury, it doesn't remove Ball from Friday's 8-9 game against the Orlando Magic and it all but certainly won't impact the Hornets should they reach the first round.

That's because one quirk of the tournament's addition is that, not unlike the NBA Cup title game, the play-in tournament lives as its own statistical entity. They are neither playoff nor regular-season games, with no bearing on postseason and regular-season stats or awards.

That's also the case with flagrant foul points, which can have a massive impact when they start to add up. In 2016, Draymond Green was suspended for Game 5 of the NBA Finals for accumulating four flagrant points over the course of the postseason, something that helped Cleveland pull off its stunning 3-1 comeback.

While the Hornets' playoff stay isn't likely to last as long -- Charlotte needs to win Friday just to set up a first-round meeting with the top-seeded Detroit Pistons -- Ball entering the playoffs with two flagrant points would have at least given heft to the belated punishment.

Instead, the decision felt fairly hollow. And in asking sources around the league Wednesday ahead of the NBA's announcement that Ball wouldn't be suspended, opinions were mixed. Some argued that a hefty fine would suffice, because you shouldn't retroactively remove him from the next game because of Adebayo's unfortunate injury. Others argued the opposite, saying he should have to sit out Friday's win-and-in showdown.

None of it, however, will reverse the agonizing end to Miami's season.

"I'm not really thinking about that anymore," Heat coach Erik Spoelstra told reporters Thursday during the team's exit interviews. "I don't think [Ball] is a dirty player. It should have been caught in the moment, and it wasn't. And you move on." -- Tim Bontemps

Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim Bontemps and Tim MacMahon to discuss the final day of the NBA regular season, including how upsets influenced the playoff seeding. Wemby reaches 65-game mark
After seeing his season cut short a year ago because of a blood clot in his right shoulder, Victor Wembanyama is now eligible for postseason awards. He reached the 65-game criterion in the San Antonio Spurs' 139-120 win over the Dallas Mavericks on Friday night. He finished with 40 points and 13 rebounds in just 26 minutes.

Wembanyama is eligible to sign a five-year, $251 million extension this offseason. Because he was ineligible for league honors last year, there are no financial implications in the extension if he were named All-NBA or Defensive Player of the Year this season.

The extension will likely include a 30% clause that increases the total amount $50 million if he is named MVP, All-NBA or Defensive Player of the Year in 2026-27.

Wembanyama has 10 games of at least 20 points and 15 rebounds this season. That trails only Tim Duncan for the most in Spurs history. He has 16 games of at least 25 points and four blocks this season, the most by any player. -- Bobby Marks

The NBA's most valuable players in 15 categories

Duren hits 65-game mark
After failing to reach an extension last offseason, the Detroit Pistons' Jalen Duren is set to cash in.

Duren, who is a restricted free agent this summer, has now reached the 65-game mark to be eligible for All-NBA honors. Entering their game against the Milwaukee Bucks, Duren had played 68 games. However, four of the games did not qualify because he played fewer than 15 minutes.

Due to a clause in the CBA, Duren and his representatives are allowed to negotiate a contract up to 30% of the maximum salary if he's named to an All-NBA team. The contract can be for up to five years and $287 million.

If Duren is not named All-NBA, he is eligible for a five-year, $239 million contract.

Duren led the NBA in total points per game and was named to the All-Star team for the first time in his career. -- Bobby Marks

Curry to miss Thursday's game, no matchups with LeBron this season
The Golden State Warriors have announced Stephen Curry will miss Thursday night's game against the Los Angeles Lakers due to it falling on a back-to-back, as the star player returns from injury.

The missed game means that Curry and LeBron James will not have met in the regular season, and they likely won't meet in the playoffs.

Embiid to undergo surgery for appendicitis
The Philadelphia 76ers announced that Joel Embiid will undergo surgery for appendicitis in Houston on Thursday afternoon. They also reported that further updates will come.

April 8

The NBA's take on tanking

ESPN's Anthony Slater talked to players, coaches and executives about how they feel about tanking in the NBA and the future it has in the league.

In ESPN's conversations with dozens of players, coaches and front office executives, a consistent theme emerged: Nobody likes it -- "I hate it," Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said -- but not many deny it is often the most prudent team-building path when stuck near the bottom. Different seasons and different drafts will generate different forms, but everyone agrees it'll continue until the NBA figures out either the proper rules or punishments to curb it.

"These teams are doing the whole gamut: sitting guys in the fourth, playing analytically bad lineups, drawing up plays for bad shots," one Western Conference general manager said. "The creativity is impressive and I don't blame them. It's the best strategy to get better. Look at all the most promising teams in the league: Thunder, Spurs, Pistons, Rockets, Hornets. Years of being bad and building up on high picks. It's painful but worthwhile."

The strategies are growing in audaciousness and frequency of use. The orders from management are coming in earlier in the season, creating months of competitively compromised and often unwatchable basketball. The average margin of victory in NBA games this season is 13.1 points, the largest spread in history, and a record 89 games have been decided by 30 or more points.

Bulls hiring search firm for front office replacements
The Chicago Bulls are expected to engage a search firm in order to find a replacement for vice president Arturas Karnisovas and general manager Marc Eversley, whom the team fired after six seasons running the basketball operations department, sources told ESPN.

It's a different approach from the process Chicago used when it hired Karnisovas in 2020. Team president and CEO Michael Resindorf said then that he targeted the top "No. 2" in basketball and went after general managers such as Karnisovas, who was then with the Denver Nuggets, and Bobby Webster, who was then general manager of the Toronto Raptors, but has since been promoted to their head of basketball operations.

This is only the second time since 2003 that the Bulls have hired a new head of basketball operations. Before Karnisovas got the job in 2020, John Paxson assumed the role for 17 years from 2003 to '20. Karnisovas and Eversley went 224-254 across six seasons leading the organization to one winning season and one playoff appearance.

Even though Chicago sits 29-49 and in 12th place in the Eastern Conference, the opening is expected to be an attractive one around the league. The Bulls have flexibility on how they can build their roster with their own lottery pick, approximately $60 million in cap space and young players on the roster without long-term salary commitments.

Chicago is still expected to try to retain coach Billy Donovan in some capacity after the season. -- Jamal Collier

Bulls fire Karnisovas, Eversley

The fractured relationship between Giannis and the Milwaukee Bucks
ESPN's Shams Charania went inside the drama between two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Milwaukee Bucks, as a crucial summer window approaches. The story details what has led to the falling out in Milwaukee and what it means for the future of both Antetokounmpo and the Bucks.

This season, the Bucks have gone 17-19 with Antetokounmpo in the lineup and 14-28 without him, and they rank 25th in offensive rating and 26th in defensive rating overall. They are one of six NBA teams to rank in the bottom five in both categories.
All the while, the uncertainty of Antetokounmpo's future in Milwaukee lingered. The Bucks engaged in trade talks ahead of the Feb. 5 trade deadline but chose to hold on to him, even as it became increasingly clear that they didn't have much hope of even elevating into the play-in race. Milwaukee is now headed to the draft lottery for the first time since 2016, snapping a streak of nine consecutive years in the playoffs. The Bucks haven't won a postseason series since 2022. Antetokounmpo, who is under contract for one more season, has played in a career-low 36 games and privately feuded with the organization for several months, culminating in rebuking the team's requests to shut down in the final month of the season and setting up another contentious summer.

"When your best player is one foot in, one foot out," said one team source, "you're not going to win."

The Bucks have officially been eliminated from the playoffs.

Doncic signed a three-year extension last August and has been named All-NBA in five of the six previous seasons.

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over eight seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would reset standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers such as Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the piñata while he's under contract.

We can tsk-tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player who logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent, Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL who believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's got to sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 million annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman who will be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He has a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the expected goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the expected goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this megadeal.

Winner: player empowerment
As I wrote in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players who take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.

stories.headline: What we learned: Pressure can win Hawks the flag; the massive warning sign for Freo
stories.summary: The Hawks' outstanding pressure can win them a premiership, but the Dockers have a big problem after a 'morale-sapping' home qualifying final loss. Here's three things we learned from Hawthorn's win over Fremantle.
stories.body:
Hawthorn produced a stunning performance Thursday evening at Optus Stadium to upset minor premier Fremantle and advance to a second successive preliminary final.

Sam Mitchell's side will now enjoy the week off before returning to the MCG to hunt a place in the 2026 AFL Grand Final. Meanwhile, the Dockers will face the winner of Geelong and Carlton next week in a must-win semifinal.

Here are three things we learned from the game:

Hawthorn's relentless pressure can win the flag
It was a masterclass of pressure and intensity from the Hawks on Thursday evening in the west as they put the Dockers to the sword on their home deck to book their ticket to the final four once again.

The Hawks played the wet-dry conditions perfectly and completely stymied the minor premiers for four quarters. Sam Mitchell's side brought the heat from the opening siren, pressing up and hunting in packs, while never allowing their opponents a moment to breathe and settle into the contest.

They locked the ball inside their attacking forward 50 and had Fremantle's back six under siege for most of the evening, forcing the Dockers into 32 defensive half turnovers -- their most in a game all year. Neither the Docker defense, nor the midfield group, had any answers to stop the onslaught as they again buckled under the finals spotlight.

Mabior Chol set the standard in the opening minutes with two gut-busting efforts inside forward 50. His fleet-footed brigade of small forwards never stood still for a second, while co-captain Jai Newcombe and Dylan Moore were in-and-under all night long, combining for 14 tackles.

It was this insatiable intent and appetite for the contest that allowed Hawthorn to pile on six consecutive goals following Luke Jackson's early opener. The Hawks took a 33-point advantage into the main break, restricting Fremantle to that lone Jackson major. The margin remained the same at the final change and could only be cut to 32 by the final siren.

Thursday's performance was proof the stat sheet can sometimes be a tad misleading. The Dockers dominated total disposals (+74) and enjoyed an advantage in inside 50s (+6), while the clearance and contested possession counts were virtually identical. And yet this game only ever looked like having one victor.

Hawthorn will now enjoy a well-earned week off before returning to the MCG for a preliminary final. The three most likely opponents for that game all reside outside Victoria. If the home crowd support can be paired with the ferocity displayed against Fremantle, there's no reason they can't jag two more wins in 2026.

We should be seriously worried about these Dockers
Fremantle had been the team of the season. Minor premiers with 19 wins and four losses. An even more imposing record at Optus Stadium where they were unbeaten in 12 games, including a sensational come-from-behind win against these Hawks back in Round 9.

Unfortunately for Justin Longmuir and the legion of fans decked head to toe in purple, the Dockers waited until September to turn in their biggest stinker of the year. The Hawks played this game like the final it was and the all-conquering home side never appeared close to being up for the occasion.

Aside from All-Australian running defender Jordan Clark and the reliable Andrew Brayshaw, Fremantle had few winners on the night. Midfielders Shai Bolton and Caleb Serong were well below their best, Murphy Reid left his kicking boots at home, while forward pair Josh Treacy and Jye Amiss were just about unsighted throughout.

Thursday evening was Fremantle's lowest score of the season (40), while the 17 points scored from turnover were the fewest they had managed in a game since 2019 (excluding season 2020 which featured shortened quarters). It was also the club's second-worst game of the year for converting scores from inside 50s.

Fremantle will now have to pick themselves up, dust themselves off, and regroup for a do-or-die semifinal against either Geelong or Carlton next weekend. And while they'll likely be favoured to win that game, would anyone be tipping them with a high degree of confidence?

The loss to the Hawks is as morale-sapping as it gets. Not only because it undoes so much of the great work that was done throughout the year. Not because for them to lift the premiership they'd have to win three straight games, including two on the other side of the country. But because this club, and its supporter base, was adamant it had turned the corner following last year's disappointing home elimination final defeat to Gold Coast.

That one-point loss to end last year's campaign could prove costly 12 months on. All of a sudden the Dockers have lost two finals in a row on their home deck and will be sweating at the prospect of it becoming three in a row next weekend. Meanwhile, what would the Cats or Blues really have to lose?

If you don't want James Sicily at his worst, you don't deserve him at his best
Sure, at times he can play the role of the ultimate villain, but Hawthorn co-captain James Sicily can also be the coolest head you're likely to find behind the ball and one of the greatest assets in football come September.

On Thursday evening he was very much the latter. Sicily was simply sensational against the Dockers, leading the defensive group that completely nullified Fremantle's dangerous three-pronged attack.

Time and time again Sicily out-positioned and out-bodied the Fremantle forwards, drawing on all of his experience and smarts to put on a defensive clinic. He was always in the right place at the right time, always a step ahead of his opponent, and always composed with Sherrin in hand.

Sicily finished his night in the west with a team-high 26 disposals, a game-high 12 intercept possessions, 10 marks, and seven score involvements -- more than any player wearing brown and gold not named Nick Watson.

"We wanted to commit to being tough and taking the game on," Sicily told Fox Sports after the win. "The way we were in sync tonight is just going to give us so much confidence."

There's more than a few Hawks that can make claims to being their club's most important player, but it's hard to look past Sicily when he's in this type of form.

stories.headline: Fernando Alonso uncertain on future: 'This is not the Formula 1 we grew up with'
stories.summary: Fernando Alonso has said his decision on whether to keep racing into 2027 with Aston Martin is still not made because "this is not the Formula 1 we grew up with."
stories.body:
Fernando Alonso has said his decision on whether to keep racing into 2027 with Aston Martin is still not made because "this is not the Formula 1 we grew up with."

Alonso's contract expires at the end of the current season and the 45-year-old has not committed to staying on.

Alonso has been one of the most out-spoken drivers about F1's new engine regulations -- which he has called the "battery world championship" because of the shift towards the electrical elements in the new hybrid engines.

Making matters worse for him was that Aston Martin has started the new rules cycle in horrible shape, with engine partner Honda massively off the pace, although Alonso managed to finish ninth at the Dutch Grand Prix, where the Japanese manufacturer introduced its first major upgrade of the season.

Alonso suggested there is a lot more stopping him from committing to a 25th season on the grid.

"For my decision it is not really about the [Aston Martin] car," Alonso said when probed on his future. "I will be professional and working at my 100%, fighting for P15 or fighting for a podium. But for me it is more about the regulations.

"Unfortunately, this is what it is. This is not the Formula 1 we grew up with. This is not the Formula 1 that we all want, drivers, spectators. So we must change a few things, it will not happen immediately. It will happen for the future. But I hope I can contribute somehow for the next set of regulations and we can go back to the real Formula 1."

Monza's Italian Grand Prix looks set to be another brutal run-out for F1's much-maligned new cars, with the layout of the circuit likely to expose the limitations of the battery elements of the new engine.

Asked if it would be up there with Suzuka and Silverstone, Alonso said: "Worse."

On whether it would be the worst of the year, he shrugged and said: "Maybe [not as bad as] Vegas."

- Monza personifies the passion that enticed Leclerc to commit his future to Ferrari

- Lightning McQueen to make F1 debut at Italian GP as safety car also gets Cars makeover

- Why does the Italian GP trophy look like a pile of washing up?

Alonso is the biggest name remaining on the driver market currently, but his options appear to be to stay with Aston Martin or retire -- Alpine's extension for Franco Colapinto, confirmed last week, closed off his most likely route out of Aston Martin should he want to take it.

Aston Martin has still promised to introduce at least one more car upgrade, while Honda's new package will be properly tested this weekend in Monza.

Although happy to have returned his colleagues to the points-paying positions, Alonso said a lot more needs to come before the end of the season to convince him to have another season of racing.

"No," he said when asked if P9 was enough for him to consider continuing. "We cannot be happy just with P9 and I think no one is happy in the team.

"It was a nice boost for everyone knowing that at least the direction that we are taking is the right one. Because we changed a lot of things in the car since Budapest. And obviously we know, we feel that in the corners we are getting in a much better place.

"So that gives hope for everyone in Silverstone that if we keep on going on this philosophy and this strategy and this pace of development, eventually we will be one of the fastest in the corners. So we tick one of the boxes. Then on the engine side, I think Zandvoort was not a big improvement to be honest.

"The drivability was a problem and the extra power was difficult to feel in Zandvoort. Maybe Monza is going to be a more true test for the engine. But it is still a long way to go."
