stories.headline: How Bueckers, Clark, Reese will impact Team USA at World Cup
stories.summary: The future is here for Team USA as Paige Bueckers, Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese and others make their debut in a major event.
stories.body:
A picture from 2017 resurfaces occasionally on social media. In it, a younger Caitlin Clark, Paige Bueckers and Aliyah Boston wear USA Basketball gear, huddling somewhere at the U.S. Olympic Training Center in Colorado Springs, Colorado, and flashing thumbs up and peace signs.

They had been in the cold tubs amid preparations for the FIBA Americas U16 Championship, Bueckers recently recalled to ESPN, probably after a dreaded two-a-day session. The photo also features Azzi Fudd -- who like the other three would later become a No. 1 WNBA draft pick -- and former Stanford standout Fran Belibi.

"We were all down bad hurting at such a young age," Bueckers said.

"I don't think any of us probably would have guessed we would have all made it [to this level], and that the WNBA is what it is now with the amount of attention that's on us," Clark told ESPN. "But at the same time, I think we would all say it's pretty cool. It's kind of like a pinch me moment."

Over the next 10 days, Clark, Bueckers and Boston will again share the court representing the United States with a slew of younger WNBA stars in Angel Reese, Kiki Iriafen and Sonia Citron at the FIBA World Cup in Berlin.

The group of transcendent players, with their on-court talent and off-court relevance, catapulted the WNBA into a new era of popularity. Now they are tasked with helping Team USA secure its 12th World Cup gold medal and fifth straight.

"There's always pride when you wear USA," Boston told ESPN. "I think it's kind of a full circle moment for us to be in the big girl jerseys now."

The future -- or as Bueckers quipped in December, the "Young and Turnt" crew -- is here. And they're perhaps even younger, and being thrown into the fire, even more than anticipated.

USA Basketball announced Monday that Team USA stalwarts A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum will not compete in Berlin due to health reasons. Those decisions led to Iriafen and Citron getting called up to join the group.

The U.S. women's team has six players under the age of 25, tied for the most on a USA World Cup or Olympic roster since 1994. With Rhyne Howard, 26, also on the squad, seven of the 12 players have never represented the senior national team in either major international 5-on-5 tournament, tied for the second-most such players on a USA roster since 1994.

But none of that matters when a gold medal is on the line. The standard for USA Basketball, which has lost one game at the World Cup or Olympics since 1994, remains the same -- even as it has become more difficult than ever to win on the international stage, as the United States' one-point win over France at the Paris Olympics' gold medal game illustrated.

"There's no question that the world is improving at a rapid rate," U.S. coach Kara Lawson said Tuesday. "I think it's going to be the most difficult World Cup to win that we've had because of that."

THE ORIGINS OF the "Young and Turnt" generation for USA Basketball might have come from that 2017 U16 team, but the players' arrival onto one of the sport's biggest stages was far from guaranteed.

Clark, Bueckers, Boston, Howard and Citron have all won multiple gold medals with USA Basketball at the youth level, from 2017 U16 gold in Argentina to finishing atop the podium at the 2019 U19 World Cup in Thailand, among others.

But as former USA Basketball national team director Carol Callan -- who oversaw all of the women's programs from 1996 to 2021 -- used to explain to players, those U17 and U19 World Cup teams would produce, on average, only one Olympian.

The World Cup is different from the Olympics, but "I think you could tell with those three specifically, they were all about basketball," Callan said of Clark, Bueckers and Boston. "Those three started at the top and they've maintained that. That's credit to them for not only their ability, but their drive, their mentality and the people that support them."

Howard has also been a mainstay for USA Basketball, featured on the Olympic qualifying team ahead of the Paris Games before ultimately being named to the 3x3 squad. Reese and Iriafen took less obvious paths: Iriafen first linked up with USA Basketball at December's training camp; Reese tried out for various youth national teams before making her first USA Basketball roster for the 2023 AmeriCup.

Callan said she ran into Reese at the event and "she just was so happy to be on a team, and I thought that was really great."

"You have two different ways to react to not making a team," Callan said. "One way is to just get angry and be done with it. And Angel persevered and made a team, and I can't say enough about her and how she's progressed to where she is today."

The sometimes-roundabout routes -- which for someone like Bueckers included missing significant time in college due to injury and falling out of the USA circuit -- makes being part of the senior national team now even sweeter.

"We all had different paths. We worked hard, had great faith. We just maintained our love and passion for the game," Bueckers said. "We're just grateful to be able to play at the national team level. Not everybody gets there. Not everybody has the same journey."

Added Clark: "I feel like there was just so much talent around my age group, and it's been fun to watch everybody kind of come into their own and have their own college careers and now live their dream at the professional level. ... It's just really cool, and feels like yesterday, honestly."

THE CHANGING OF the guard for USA Basketball started well before Berlin. The 2022 World Cup in Sydney was the USA's first major international competition since 2002 without Sue Bird or Diana Taurasi. Bird had announced her retirement, while Taurasi was injured.

Taurasi and Brittney Griner, who missed the 2022 World Cup while detained in Russia, were the most experienced members in Paris two years ago, though controversially neither saw much if any playing time in the final.

Breanna Stewart and Wilson had become the face of the USA Basketball dynasty, combining to win the past two MVPs at each of the Olympics and World Cup. The duo also accounted for 41% of the scoring at the Paris Games.

"We don't have that vet person; we are those people now," Stewart said recently.

Already a three-time Olympic gold medalist, Stewart, who recently turned 32, has a chance to join Bird as the only players to win four World Cup gold medals. She made her World Cup debut in 2014 at age 20.

"We are the ones who have been around the block a few times," Stewart told ESPN, "and it's exciting to help lead and guide them."

While a relatively inexperienced group, the United States is considered the favorite in Berlin, its roster loaded with young talent. Of the seven newcomers making their debut in a major international 5-on-5 competition, four were No. 1 picks in the WNBA draft and recent rookies of the year: Howard (2022), Boston (2023), Clark (2024) and Bueckers (2025).

Clark, Reese and Howard are leading the WNBA in assists (8.4), rebounds (12.4), and steals (2.4) per game, respectively. Clark and Bueckers are two of six players averaging at least 20 points. Citron and Iriafen are already multitime All-Stars despite being second-year players.

Clark, Bueckers, Reese, Howard and Iriafen already got a taste of what it's like to play for the senior national team, and Lawson, in March at the World Cup Qualifying tournament. In all, eight USA players who were in Puerto Rico -- including Chelsea Gray, Kahleah Copper and Jackie Young -- will also compete in Berlin. Clark and Bueckers were two of three players (alongside Plum) to play over 100 minutes in Puerto Rico and two of the top-four scorers for Team USA. Clark's 6.4 assists per game led the entire field, propelling her to earn MVP of the event.

Lawson has lauded Clark's play for the Indiana Fever this season, while the guard has said she hopes to be an extension of Lawson on the floor.

"They're both terrific," Lawson said while calling a WNBA game last month between Bueckers and Clark for Prime Video. "They're both about winning, which I think is the most important attribute in a player, in a great player."

While Clark and Bueckers might be the backcourt of the future, the ball is still expected to be primarily in the hands of Gray, the eldest player on the team at 33 and a two-time Olympic and 2022 World Cup gold medalist. But the younger guards will be watching closely to learn from her -- "I'll probably be annoying, I'll be asking so many questions," Bueckers said recently.

Stewart will anchor the effort in the frontcourt, but Reese, Boston and Iriafen will undoubtedly have even more responsibility now with Wilson out. Lawson has praised Reese for her impact on the glass -- her 8.0 boards in 16.7 minutes per game in Puerto Rico were second most in the tournament -- but has also said she sees the Dream star's physicality and competitive fire as translating well onto the FIBA stage.

"I just enjoy how she raises the level of a practice or of a game with her presence and with her intensity," Lawson said. "She plays with an aggression and a physicality, which I think is really important in FIBA play because there's a little more aggression and physicality that's typically allowed relative to the WNBA, and you need to have players that embrace that, and I think she's definitely one of the players on the roster that embraces that."

The combination of so much newness -- even Lawson was tabbed coach about a year ago -- and so little prep time is never ideal going into a major tournament, but that is typically how USA Basketball is forced to operate. The players and staff will lean on their time together in Puerto Rico or at training camps sprinkled across the past 10 months.

But they can also lean on the qualities that got them to Berlin. Lawson said her message to the younger players is to be themselves, and keep their mindset, confidence and belief in who they are intact no matter their role or experience.

"While they are kind of rookies, in my mind they're veterans," Callan said. "They infuse a competitiveness and an appreciation for the game that I think matches most those wily old veterans. You want some young ones that have this sort of really fun outlook on it, and I think they do [at the right times]. ... I think they'll bring a really nice mix to this team."

stories.headline: Fenerbahce: Mason Greenwood, Matteo Guendouzi subject of UEFA investigation
stories.summary: Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi are the subject of a disciplinary investigation by UEFA, Fenerbahce have confirmed.
stories.body:
Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi are the subject of a disciplinary investigation by UEFA, Fenerbahce have confirmed.

Fenerbahce's 2-1 win away at Lyon in a Champions League qualifier ended amid ugly scenes involving Greenwood and Guendouzi who both previously played for Marseille, the rivals of Lyon.

Guendouzi raised his middle finger to Lyon fans during the warmup and after the game and shouted "Allez l'OM" ("Go Marseille"), also grabbing his crotch, in wild post-match scenes. He said Lyon fans insulted his family before and during the game.

A post-match scuffle included someone wearing Lyon club colours confronting Guendouzi, before several players became involved in an incident in the tunnel.

It was unclear if UEFA's disciplinary judges will sanction the players before Fenerbahce opens the Champions League main phase next Thursday, hosting Roma. Fenerbahce's second game is at Aston Villa on Oct. 14.

A Fenerbahce statement read: "Following the UEFA Champions League playoff round second leg match, UEFA has initiated disciplinary proceedings against our players Matteo Guendouzi and Mason Greenwood, as well as against our club.

"Our club will present the necessary defences before the relevant UEFA bodies in order to protect the rights and interests of our players and Fenerbahce during this process.

"The necessary information, documents and defences regarding the process will be submitted to UEFA, and developments are being closely monitored by our club. We hereby inform the public."

Fenerbahce qualified for the Champions League for the first time since 2008-09 at Lyon's expense after a 3-2 aggregate win.

Former Manchester United striker Greenwood joined the Turkish club this summer from Marseille in a €39 million ($44.5m) deal.

stories.headline: Broncos fall to 45-year low despite defeating Bulldogs
stories.summary: Canterbury have rolled over with a whimper in their final NRL regular-season game as the Bulldogs fell to Brisbane in a 34-20 defeat.
stories.body:
Brisbane have brought the curtain down on their miserable NRL premiership defence with a 34-20 victory over Canterbury.

Eleven months on from their drought-breaking title, the Broncos returned to Accor Stadium on Thursday and sent Payne Haas out as a winner in his final Brisbane game before he joins South Sydney.

Haas, one of the heroes of last year's premiership, scored the opening try and was sent to the sin bin in an eventful first half that ended 10-10.

But after halftime Brisbane, who have been out of finals contention for weeks, pulled away and piled on 24 second-half points.

The victory was just Brisbane's eighth for the season, in what represents the worst return of any defending premiers since Canterbury in 1981.

The Broncos are just the third side in the NRL era to miss the finals in the year after a premiership.

Winger Josiah Karapani was a standout for the Broncos on Thursday, scoring two tries, chalking up 142m and 13 tackle busts as Canterbury's season ended with a whimper.

A large contingent of Bulldogs fans in the official crowd of 13,802 headed for the exit on the hour mark, and it would be hard to blame them after a year when it felt Canterbury took a step backwards by missing out on the top eight.

As has been the case for much of this season, the Bulldogs' attack was pedestrian and laboured, and even with 38 play-the-balls in Brisbane's 20m zone they struggled to threaten in possession.

Halfback Lachlan Galvin was one of those try-scorers - hitting back after Haas and Karapani gave Brisbane an early lead - but his suitability to wear the No. 7 alongside Stephen Crichton at five-eighth is sure to be a dominant storyline over the off-season.

Crichton had a hand in Canterbury's second through left winger Enari Tuala to level the scores going into halftime, but Brisbane kicked on from there.

Billy Walters, Ben Hunt, Jordan Riki and Karapani all touched down in the 20 minutes after halftime to give Brisbane their third win since a round-eight defeat of the Bulldogs in April.

Viliame Kikau and Galvin scored two late tries to reduce the deficit, but the fulltime scoreline flattered Canterbury, who finish the year with an 11-13 record.

stories.headline: Chiefs rush to rebuild defense around veteran Chris Jones
stories.summary: First-round picks Peter Woods and R Mason Thomas are bringing plenty of heat, which can only help Jones.
stories.body:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- This summer for Chris Jones was different.

The realization really hit Jones, the Chiefs' star pass rusher, in early June, when he kept looking around in the huddle. He was reminded again in early August, during one of the Chiefs' first fully-padded practices. A large number of the reps taken featured Jones lined up next to rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods, the Chiefs' second of two first-round picks. On the other side of Jones, the defensive end sometimes was R Mason Thomas, another rookie, this one the Chiefs selected in the draft's second round.

Of course, Jones is aware that Woods, 21, and Thomas, 22, are a decade younger than him. And of course, one of the teammates Woods and Thomas have gravitated to the most ahead of the upcoming season is Jones, who at age 32 is the Chiefs' best defender -- and their longest-tenured, too.

"That's a nice way to say you're old," Jones said, laughing. "I've been in the league going on 11 years, so, I mean, if they paid attention to the Chiefs any bit, then they've probably seen me on the field."

Youth is just one element of the Chiefs' changes on defense. Even Jones' fellow starting interior lineman is Khyiris Tonga, who joined the team in free agency. All those major changes surrounding Jones -- who has always been the sun around which the Chiefs defense has revolved during their dynastic run -- were what the Chiefs believe this offseason was necessary for the franchise to return to contention after missing the playoffs for the first time since 2014.

No other part of the roster received as many newcomers, draft capital and overhaul from the previous year than along the Chiefs' defensive line. In fact, Woods and Thomas are the first duo of defensive linemen the Chiefs selected in the first and second rounds of the same draft since 2002 (defensive tackle Ryan Sims and defensive end Eddie Freeman). All those efforts, led by coach Andy Reid, general manager Brett Veach and longtime coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, were made to fix one of the team's biggest issues: the pass rush.

"Besides Chris, you want guys that can [get] pressure," Reid said. "If you leave these quarterbacks [time] in this league, and let them sit there [in the pocket], they're going to rip you apart. You've got to make them uncomfortable -- and you have to have the guys to be able to do that.

"The guys Brett bought in have that ability. It's just a matter of getting it done."

Unlike any previous year under Spagnuolo, who joined the Chiefs in 2019, this year's path for the defense to be its most effective is expected to be made through the improved production of the linemen.

In early August, one particular rep was a glimpse of what the Chiefs hope to see plenty in the future. With the offense in a passing situation, quarterback Patrick Mahomes received the snap from the shotgun. One side of the Chiefs' pass rush was Jones and defensive end George Karlaftis, the four-year veteran and team's most experienced and accomplished edge rusher. Woods and Thomas worked from the left side. Together, the four players -- and an overload blitz with two extra defenders -- were able to pressure Mahomes, forcing the quarterback to throw a short pass in less than two seconds. The result of the play was an interception by nickel cornerback Chris Roland-Wallace.

The following week, during camp's hardest stretch, something occurred that rarely happened last season: Jones was on the sideline -- and the defense was still able to beat the offensive line's protection. In a matchup against left tackle Josh Simmons, Woods was able to leap in the air and use his right hand to knock down Mahomes' pass without touching the quarterback. When the play was over, the second-closest defender next to Mahomes was Thomas.

"We got some dawgs in the room," Jones said. "Peter Woods, I love that guy. He's a young bull. R Mason is going to contribute a lot for us in the pass rush."

Later this month, the Chiefs will open their season on "Monday Night Football" against the Denver Broncos. Much of the Chiefs' 2026 campaign -- after finishing last season with an underwhelming 6-11 record -- will be determined by the play of Mahomes, who is on track to be the team's starter for Week 1 after recovering from the torn ACL and LCL in his left knee.

For Jones, he was blunt when he shared how he will measure the defense's overall performance, the one statistic he believes has to change the most.

"We've got to get more sacks," Jones said after the Chiefs had just 35, the fifth fewest in the league, last season, including just 21.5 recorded by the D-line. "It affected the defense tremendously. If we want this defense to be a success, we've got to get more sacks."

ALMOST A YEAR ago, the troubling signs for the Chiefs' pass rush were evident as early as their first game.

In São Paulo, the Chiefs barely touched Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert when they didn't blitz (their two sacks were a byproduct of sending extra defenders). Frustrated by being double-teamed for most of the game -- and the lack of pressure from his fellow teammates -- Jones switched positions and lined up on the edge to get a one-on-one matchup for the Chargers' pivotal third-and-14 snap. With the Chargers leading by six points, Spagnuolo's unit was one play away from giving the ball back to Mahomes for a potential game-winning drive.

However, Jones wanted to get pressure on Herbert so quickly that he lost outside contain, allowing the quarterback to scramble near the sideline for a 19-yard gain. Jones' mistakes, which he acknowledged after the game, led to a verbal confrontation between him and linebacker Drue Tranquill.

As the Chiefs lost one-score game after one-score game -- finishing last season with a league-worst 1-9 record in such games -- the burden grew larger and larger for Jones: If he didn't impact the quarterback, his D-line teammates, other than Karlaftis, didn't provide much help.

Against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Jones played 48 of 58 total snaps, the most of any defensive lineman. Jones showed that he was fatigued in the midst of the Jaguars' game-winning drive in the final minute, his final snap his most embarrassing. Quarterback Trevor Lawrence stumbled under center with the Jaguars at the 1-yard line trailing by four with just 30 seconds left. Jones, realizing he was going to be double-teamed again, didn't pursue Lawrence with maximum effort. A few seconds later, Jones watched Lawrence get up and scramble across the goal line for the winning touchdown.

"This year, I plan to start high -- and go higher," said Jones, who led the Chiefs last season with seven sacks.

Karlaftis struggled in the second half of the season, too, recording only one sack in his final seven games while he played through a nagging thumb injury. In November, during a four-game stretch, the Chiefs' defensive ends combined to get only one sack.

"It was a humbling offseason," Karlaftis said. "It was the first offseason not coming off a Super Bowl [appearance]. I had to get my mind right. There was a month there that I was kind of looking at the man in the mirror and trying to figure out how I can help do my part so that what happened last year never happens again."

Veach had a similar feeling. Most of the roster moves he made last season for the pass rush failed. Veach re-signed Charles Omenihu and Mike Danna, both of whom helped the Chiefs win two Super Bowls. Jerry Tillery and Janarius Robinson joined the team, too. None of them made significant contributions.

The plan for the interior resulted in a bizarre outcome. The Chiefs didn't re-sign Derrick Nnadi after the 2024 season, choosing to retain Mike Pennel. But the Chiefs released Pennel after the preseason and then made a small trade with the New York Jets to acquire Nnadi. Once it was clear Nnadi wasn't an upgrade, the Chiefs in late October re-signed Pennel, who was released after playing eight games for the Cincinnati Bengals.

Another reason Pennel rejoined the Chiefs was because Omarr Norman-Lott sustained a season-ending torn ACL in his right knee. Prior to the injury, Norman-Lott, the 2025 second-round pick, showed some pass-rushing potential -- skills the Chiefs were hoping to further cultivate with more snaps in the second half of the season.

Too often, Spagnuolo was forced to blitz, a tactic offenses found easy ways to outwit. Although the Chiefs blitzed on 192 snaps (seventh most in the league), they allowed 7.2 yards per play (tied for fourth most), according to TruMedia. The Chiefs' 43.6% third-down conversion rate also ranked 29th.

"Getting after the quarterback with four is significant," said Brandon Thorn, the creator of "Trench Warfare," a website dedicated to analysis of offensive and defensive line play. "I think the love of corners and exotic blitzes has been at least partly, I would speculate, just sheer necessity because he hasn't had the dudes up front to win rushing four.

"The addition of Thomas and Woods signal they may have had enough of having to manufacture [pressure] and rely on [Jones] as much as they have."

THE SHIFT WITHIN the Chiefs' defense, and placing more of an emphasis on the front four, began March 4. That day, the Chiefs traded cornerback Trent McDuffie, a two-time All-Pro and their second-best defender, to the Los Angeles Rams for a package of four draft picks, including the No. 29 overall selection in this year's draft.

The move by Veach, although it was difficult, was one that he had done before. In the 2022 offseason, the Chiefs began the second phase of their dynastic run by trading receiver Tyreek Hill, a three-time All-Pro at the time, to the Miami Dolphins in exchange for five draft picks.

Entering that year's draft with 12 picks, Veach used the Chiefs' two first-round picks to acquire McDuffie and Karlaftis. That draft class also included reliable defenders such as safety Bryan Cook, linebacker Leo Chenal and cornerback Jaylen Watson, all of whom left the Chiefs in free agency this offseason.

Once again, Veach knew what he had to do after trading McDuffie.

"We've got to nail these picks," Veach said before the draft.

The Chiefs' biggest swing in hoping to add another star player next to Jones in this year's draft didn't occur in the opening round. Instead, that moment happened in the second round with Thomas, who, listed at 6-foot-2 and 249 pounds, is not the ideal size that Spagnuolo often prefers with his edge rusher (6-foot-3 or taller and at least 265 pounds).

At Oklahoma, though, Thomas' burst was undeniable, leading him to collect 22 sacks in his final two college seasons.

The Chiefs have learned that Thomas' tenacity is just as evident in the film room as when he's on the field. Throughout his college career, Thomas studied Broncos edge rusher Nik Bonitto, who influenced him to play at Oklahoma. Other NFL players Thomas has admired -- and adapted parts of their playing style -- are Micah Parsons (Green Bay Packers), Von Miller (Dallas Cowboys), Dallas Turner (Minnesota Vikings) and even Hall of Famer Dwight Freeney. He enjoys figuring out what nuances, such as their alignment and what information from the offense they identified before the snap of the ball, have led to their success.

"Technique outweighs the weight room a little bit," Thomas said. "You can be Hercules, right? [If] you don't bring your feet underneath yourself or you're falling down or your splits are too wide, [proper] technique kind of saves you when you may not be the ideal strength."

Thorn believes Thomas is the Chiefs' first defensive end with elite quickness and bend since former outside linebacker Dee Ford, who last played in Kansas City in 2018.

"If R Mason Thomas can do something opposite of Karlaftis, it would give them a speed guy," Thorn said. "That dynamic, theoretically now, is more in place than it has been since Tamba Hali and Justin Houston. We'll see in six, seven weeks what [Thomas] looks like."

In camp and the preseason, Thomas has proven to be a quick study.

In one-on-one drills, Thomas was able to surprise Simmons, leading the former first-round pick to say that he needed to time his pass set with the exact moment of the snap to have the proper angle to block his teammate. Thomas demonstrated a couple times he could hold his own against tight ends when the Rams ran the ball toward him in the preseason opener. The next week, Thomas generated quick pressure off the edge and he made an impressive leaping deflection on a pass that was meant for a bubble screen. And in the preseason finale against the Seattle Seahawks, Thomas overwhelmed two blockers, left tackle Logan Brown and tight end Elijah Arroyo, to sack quarterback Jalen Milroe -- who fumbled the ball -- in less than three seconds.

"He's got some stuff you just can't teach," Woods said of Thomas. "That makes my job easier. That's going to make him a better player, being able to use those [skills] that are just God-given. I'm really excited about him."

The Chiefs' final two exhibition games also showcased Woods' potential to present quality pass-rushing juice while playing next to Jones.

After not missing a practice in camp while battling a left ankle injury, Woods' athleticism was easy to notice against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Seahawks. While Thomas was pressuring the quarterback from the edge, Woods was pushing the pocket from the interior. When the Seahawks tried to run between the tackles, Woods used his footwork, quickness and agility to evade being blocked by Brown and left guard Christian Haynes, to tackle running back Jacardia Wright for no gain.

"You see the efforts the front office and the coaches made in the draft, going defense, defense, defense, like they did with Trent and I in 2022," Karlaftis said of Woods and Thomas. "Those guys are going to be studs. They have the right mind frame. They're humble, they want to work and they listen. You can't ask much more from a rookie."

Before the preseason, Woods was one of the Chiefs' most stellar performers in camp. Woods created several highlights in the trenches, sometimes even blowing by All-Pro center Creed Humphrey on 11-on-11 reps for running back Kenneth Walker III. Listed at 6-foot-3 and 310 pounds, Woods even surprised Mahomes when he was able to sprint and chase down the quarterback to end a rep.

"He's got a little bit of that alpha dog in him," Spagnuolo said of Woods. "He's got a serious tone about him that I really, really like."

Recognizing Woods' talent, Jones has been eager to be the rookie's main mentor. Jones has been pleased with how much Woods is willing to learn from him. After a fully padded practice last week, Jones spent several minutes on the field with Woods, the two going through a variety of pass-rushing techniques. Woods played the role of an offensive lineman so that Jones could demonstrate when to use certain swim moves or the footwork needed to evade a lineman's hands to better set up an outside rush move.

"I value it a lot," Woods said of Jones' expertise. "That's a future Hall of Famer that I have an opportunity to learn from and play beside. Every opportunity that we've been given to have one-on-one time together and talk through things and bounce knowledge off each other, he's been super willing, almost even initiating for that to happen. I'm very appreciative."

IN EARLY MARCH, on the same day that Walker, the reigning Super Bowl MVP, agreed to join the Chiefs, the team also made perhaps its most underrated move of the offseason: adding defensive tackle Tonga.

Veach signed Tonga, a five-year veteran, to a three-year, $21 million contract, including $14 million guaranteed. Last season, Tonga, 30, was a steady force in the middle of the New England Patriots defensive line, helping the team reach the Super Bowl. His strength at the point of attack made it easier for the Patriots to control the line of scrimmage. In the Patriots' postseason run, Tonga helped crush the pocket at times, recording seven tackles, one sack and two quarterback hits.

"This is the biggest addition to the defensive line, for sure, because we've seen him play as a pro," Thorn said. "Tonga, we know, can stop the run. It just adds flexibility for third down when he comes off the field. You can be more dynamic now."

In camp, Tonga proved his value when competing against Humphrey, pushing the center backward at times that even Joe Cullen, the defensive line coach, said he hadn't seen in his five years with the team.

"Being with Chris, plays are going to come," Tonga said. "It just elevates all of us to be better in our roles."

The Chiefs are confident that Tonga, whom Cullen described as a quiet assassin, can provide legitimate relief for Jones, who played 762 snaps last season. With Tonga expected to be on the field on first- and second-down snaps, the Chiefs know an ideal scenario would lead to Jones to play fewer snaps than last season but have him be more impactful on critical third downs. Woods' presence and development should also help Jones stay fresh for the fourth quarter of close games, when he is expected to be the defense's closer to protect the lead on the scoreboard.

"I'm 99% confident that he can have a double-digit sack season," Thorn said of Jones. "If you watch his pressures in relation to every other defensive tackle in the NFL, he is still, in my opinion, the best pass-rushing defensive tackle in the league. He had 43 high-quality pressures last season, which was more than any [other] defensive tackle in the NFL.

"Chris is still as lethal as anyone in football."

One of the most revealing days last season for Jones was in early November, when the Chiefs fell to the Buffalo Bills. Quarterback Josh Allen finished the game completing 88.5% of his passes, the highest percentage in team history (minimum 15 attempts). After the game, Jones voiced his frustration.

"We've got to take advantage of one-on-one [matchups]," Jones said that night. "When we get a single block, you've got to win."

In addition to the new players on the roster, the Chiefs have reasons for optimism that the linemen who will orbit around Jones this season -- even the rotational members -- can win more of their individual matchup in the trenches.

One backup to watch is Felix Anudike-Uzomah, the 2023 first-round pick who missed all of last season after having surgery on his right hamstring. In the preseason, Anudike-Uzomah flashed his improved athleticism with a fast, blind-side sack of Buccaneers quarterback Jake Browning. Anudike-Uzomah, who is in the final year of his rookie contract, could be the starter opposite Karlaftis on opening night against the Broncos.

"He really wants it," Karlaftis said of Anudike-Uzomah's potential for a breakout season. "He feels this is his chance, his moment. He's got a lot to prove and he knows it. He's doing everything he can to improve and show not just Kansas City, but the whole league what he's got."

Two second-year players, Norman-Lott and defensive end Ashton Gillotte, are expected to make valuable contributions later this season. Norman-Lott hopes to be activated from the physically unable to perform list before October, which would be his return to the field less than a year after sustaining his knee injury. Gillotte is rehabbing from a ruptured plantar fascia. The Chiefs think Gillotte, if his rehab goes well, has a chance to be available against the Broncos.

Healthy again himself, Karlaftis has vowed to be a better pass rusher this season, returning to the form he had in 2023, when he had a career-high 10.5 sacks and a forced fumble.

"It starts with our group," Karlaftis said of the D-line. "We can take this defense wherever we want as a front. We want to get back to the promised land. We want to get back to getting all those sacks."

stories.headline: Ismaïla Sarr will need time to process failed Liverpool move - Crystal Palace's Pierre Sage
stories.summary: Ismaïla Sarr will need time to process his proposed move to Liverpool collapsing, Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage has said.
stories.body:
Ismaïla Sarr will need time to process his proposed move to Liverpool collapsing, Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage has said.

The Senegal forward, who was Palace's top scorer last term, seemed to be closing in on a move to Anfield in the final days of the transfer window but ended up staying at Selhurst Park.

"He has to digest for sure because it's a dream for a lot of players to play with this kind of club [Liverpool]," Sage said ahead of Palace's weekend trip to Fulham.

"He had a good opportunity but in the end it didn't work.

"If he wants to continue, you have to have a good season with us as he did last year. We know he needs time.

"Like every bad situation, time does the job and we need time for that."

Sources told ESPN that Liverpool were prepared to sanction the exit of Cody Gakpo if they could find a suitable replacement.

Sarr and Brighton's Yankuba Minteh were among the names that the Reds sounded out, but they were unable to agree a fee with either club.

Liverpool therefore rejected an £80 million ($108m) bid for Gakpo from Manchester City on Monday, sources said.

The Reds did complete the signing of Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain for £106m ($144m) plus £17m ($23m) in potential performance-based add-ons.

- Liverpool needed to add depth in the transfer window. They didn't get it

- Andoni Iraola: Bradley Barcola could make Liverpool debut against Ipswich

- Honest Ahanor joins Crystal Palace on loan, will join Chelsea in 2027

On missing out on winger target Malick Fofana, who ended up joining Sunderland on deadline day, Sage said: "We gave our best. At the end of the day the player chose his criteria and I wish him and them the best because he's a good guy and a good player."

Palace travel to Fulham on Saturday with both sides still seeking their first Premier League point after two games.

Information from PA and ESPN's Beth Lindop contributed to this report.

stories.headline: 'The Hoop Collective': Episodes of Brian Windhorst's NBA podcast
stories.summary: Here are the top highlights from Brian Windhorst's "The Hoop Collective" podcast, from breaking news to the latest intel and reaction from around the NBA.
stories.body:
"The Hoop Collective" podcast, hosted by ESPN's Brian Windhorst, releases episodes every Monday, Wednesday and Friday during the NBA season and Tuesday and Friday during the offseason. Windhorst and his guests break down what's happening on and off the court, evaluating the trends you need to know and examining the latest news from across the NBA.

Listen to 'The Hoop Collective':

ESPN | Spotify | YouTube | Apple | Amazon | iHeartMedia | TuneIn

Latest episodes:

Sept. 3 | Sept. 1 |Aug. 28 | Aug. 25 | Aug. 21

Quick links:

Schedule | Standings | Stats | Transactions

'The Hoop Collective' episodes

Sept. 3: EMERGENCY POD: NBA announces Clippers' punishments after Kawhi probe
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to react to the hefty punishments handed down to the LA Clippers by the NBA after the investigation into Kawhi Leonard's off-court dealings. They break down what this means for the future of the Clippers, if the punishment makes sense and if this will impact Leonard's pending trade to the Toronto Raptors.

Topics:

1:25: NBA punishes Clippers after Kawhi probe

7:04 :The Clippers' argument against the NBA in this

10:36: What sticks out about the NBA's findings

16:47: What comes next for the Clippers?

30:21: How will this punishment impact Kawhi?

32:56: Who was most impacted by this punishment?

43:56: Final thoughts on this punishment decision

MacMahon on why the penalty was so large for the Clippers: "The simple fact of the matter is this ain't the first time Steve Balmer's pulled this shady stuff. That did not help his case.

"They gave him a little slap on the wrist for the DeAndre Jordan stuff in 2015. $250,000 fine. It was 'Oh, whoops. We didn't know.' And then, there's the investigation for the Kawhi signing because, guess what? It's not like Uncle Dennis only asked the Clippers for a whole bunch of under-the-table stuff. He was asking everybody for under-the-table stuff. 'Oh, geez. You know, we were asked, but we didn't, you know, didn't give him anything' and and now this. So, in a way they're three-time losers."

Windhorst on the Clippers' best course of action following the ruling: "If they could get an agreement, if they could plead guilty, get an agreement and and say, 'We're not going to challenge any of these penalties.' And they get an agreement that there'll be no further penalties -- basically, they'll say that these five first-round picks are all-encompassing, they cover everything. It's a blanket agreement and [then] they keep their nose clean, and they do the Kawhi trade, they might be able to come out of this without four broken limbs. They may be able to come out of this with less damage."

MacMahon on one of the winners of the investigation: "I do think Adam Silver in a way is a winner of this because straight up, he had been soft on crime as the commissioner since, ironically, he booted the previous Clippers owner, which was completely different circumstances."

Sept. 1: How Steph Curry can decide Warriors' future and major questions for Pistons
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon and Anthony Slater to discuss Stephen Curry's future with the Golden State Warriors, including how a potential extension could determine the franchise's outlook. They then move on to the Jalen Duren-Detroit Pistons situation, as his restricted free agency continues. Will this cause major issues for the Pistons' season? They close on the recent dramatic FIBA World Cup qualifiers, including a matchup between Victor Wembanyama and Nikola Jokic.

Topics:

2:09: Latest on Steph Curry's future in Golden State

8:31: How Steph could help the Warriors' chances

20:16: Jalen Duren and Pistons still stuck in negotiations

26:13: What is the worst-case scenario for Detroit?

40:40: Windy Storytime: Cavs contract standoff

46:06: Headlines from FIBA World Cup qualifiers

46:48: Epic battle between Wembanyama and Jokic

49:39: Other NBA stars making an impact in FIBA

Slater on the potential Curry extension in Golden State and why he could wait: "One of the things in discussions I've been having with people is this idea of, let's say he's like, '[Taking less money for the team is] something I'd think about.' I would be surprised if he locked into a number now because, as you just saw with Draymond Green, the Warriors and their legendary figures are willing to trust each other in business.

"Draymond Green willingly gave up $27 million and went into unrestricted free agency where he couldn't have got $27 million back, [but] under the understanding if business didn't work out, he would get that money back. If you're Steph, you say, 'OK, you know what? I'll give y'all a crack at going and trying to find some stuff, but if you don't, at the end of the day, if I come back and say, give me the full max, I get the full max.'

"So, to answer your question, he doesn't have to necessarily lock into it now because they can't really execute [upgrading the roster]. Even if they could say, 'Hey, here's a theory of what we could do. Here's another theory of what we could do,' he could just say, 'All right, well, I'll hold off for now and see if you can do it, but at the end of the day, if I want the max, give me the max.'"

MacMahon on the Duren-Detroit situation: "He just averaged 19 [points] and 11 [rebounds]. He's a big physical force with some skill. Unfortunately, and this is part of the complications here, is he also just had a really disappointing playoff performance. I would say in terms of individual playoff performances coming off of that All-NBA season, Jalen Duren might have been the most disappointing in the league.

" ... I've talked to just executives from other teams around the league just kind of taking people's temperature and a lot of what I got is like, 'I can definitely see both sides of this,' because for the Pistons this is not an anti-Jalen Duren thing. This is a, 'We want to keep this core together.' By the way, they're also in the process of attempting to negotiate an extension with Ausar Thompson."

MacMahon on the Wembanyama-Jokic rivalry: "As much as Denver's summer was frankly a disaster, you can't just dismiss the Nuggets.

"Let me say this, Victor Wembanyama might be the most dominant defensive player in the history of the game. One guy he does not bother much is Nikola Jokic. Do you know what Joker's stats against Wemby are in seven games in the NBA? 37.3 points per game, 10.9 rebounds, 9.1 assists."

Aug. 28: Kuminga's move to Minnesota and NBA awards predictions

Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to discuss Jonathan Kuminga's move to the Minnesota Timberwolves and how he'll fit with their new-look roster. They then move on to Bennedict Mathurin's deal with the New Orleans Pelicans and Shaedon Sharpe's recent injury in Portland before closing on ESPN's NBA Summer Forecast.

Windhorst on the Timberwolves' offseason and Kuminga's deal: "[Coach] Chris Finch definitely played a role [in signing Kuminga]. Obviously, I'm sure there were other Wolves that were involved as well, but obviously Ant, from what I understand, Ant was very excited. Ant, from what I am told, is very pleased by the Wolves' offseason. Going to get LaMelo [Ball], making this deal happen for Kuminga.

"I don't think Ant's a guy who stews and is angry, [but] the last time we saw Ant he was congratulating the other team with five minutes on the clock or whatever it was. I don't think he was thrilled with that situation."

MacMahon on what Minnesota needs from Kuminga: "I think a lot of this comes down to Kuminga's willingness to adapt his game to try to be a complementary player to try to fit in. There's going to be spacing concerns.

"He's not a great shooter. Jaden McDaniels' 3-point shot has kind of been up and down over the years. I think that's going to be critical. Now, Ant's a hell of a shooter. LaMelo Ball,you're going to guard him and you're going to guard him out to 30-plus feet because he'll launch it. And the percentages aren't awesome, but he's a threat, for sure. But with [Rudy] Gobert and Kuminga, you know Finch is going to have to figure out some spacing issues, but Kuminga's got to be a finisher. He's got to get off this idea that he's a ball-in-hand creator."

Aug. 25: Did Miami solve its biggest problem? Mavs building around Flagg and questions for Timberwolves

Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to break down the Klay Thompson buyout in Dallas and his deal with the Miami Heat, including whether the Heat solved their biggest problem and where they now land in the Eastern Conference. They move on to what it means for the future of the Dallas Mavericks and Cooper Flagg before closing on an ownership change in Minnesota and why this season is critical for the future of Anthony Edwards and the franchise.

Topics:

0:46: Windy Storytime: Tracy McGrady recruiting

9:04: Klay exits Dallas, signs with the Heat

25:40: Assessing the strength of Miami's roster

31:54: How are the Mavs building around Flagg?

Windhorst on how the Heat improved their chances this offseason: "When the Giannis [Antetokounmpo] trade happened, people were saying, "They've got to get shooting. They've got to get shooting." Well, Klay made 202 threes last year. Klay played 69 games last year. He made 3-pointers. Tim Hardaway [Jr.] played 80 games last year. Made 224 3-pointers. I have no idea how many games they're going to play this season. They're both in their 30s. I have no idea how many 3s they're going to hit. But these two guys combined hit [426] 3-pointers last year. And the Heat got them for $12 million combined.

"That's just good business, and if you're if you're gonna have Bam [Adebayo] and Giannis, how do you get out of that? And also, I'll point out, the [Andrew] Wiggins thing. Wiggins had a very good 3-point shooting season last year. Wiggins, [shot] 41%, I believe. That's his career high. He made 138 3-pointers. So, between the three of them, and again, this is last year, not playing together. They were playing on three different teams. I'm not saying they're going to get the same amount, but last year, between the three of them, they made 564 threes. So I don't think you can say that the Heat have a problem with 3-point shooting anymore."

MacMahon on the Mavericks' new roster: "Obviously this roster is very much a work in progress. What they did this summer, it was a lot of singles. They extended Naji Marshall. They traded for [Santi] Aldama using an exception from the AD deal. You know, they traded for [Zaccharie] Risacher. I forgot exactly where that exception came from. They traded for Marcus Sasser on another exception. You know, these are all singles, like the Risacher thing. It's a single that you're hoping you can leg that thing out and get a double out of it. It's a it's obviously an upside play for a guy who was a No. 1 pick.

"Tough to be the No. 1 pick sandwich between [Victor] Wembanyama and [Cooper] Flagg, but that's what he was. There's a reason the Hawks were willing to part with him after a couple seasons, but ,you know, 6-foot-10, has some potential there. But nothing about the Mavericks is about next season. This is about trying to build long-term around a kid who's still 19 years old in Cooper Flagg."

Windhorst on the hurdles facing the Timberwolves next offseason: "There are two people that the Wolves have to worry about keeping. [General manager] Tim Connelly, because he's been so important, and then that's second to keeping Anthony Edwards. And they're a team that has traded away draft capital and they're really going heavy. They went heavy in on LaMelo Ball. So they need the LaMelo Ball and Edwards partnership to work. They need their investment in Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert to work. They need Ant Edwards to resign next year."

Aug. 21: Cavs go all-in, what's next in Denver and updates on the Lakers situation
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon and Dave McMenamin to break down the multiteam trade that sent Peyton Watson to the Cleveland Cavaliers and Max Strus to the LA Clippers, including what it means for all the teams involved and how it led to the James Harden extension in Cleveland. Windhorst on the potential of the Watson deal in Cleveland: "In January and February, Peyton Watson went on an 18-game stretch where he started all 18 games. He averaged 36 minutes. This is a guy who averaged in the low to mid-20s before that. So he was getting full-on starters minutes. I don't have this looked up, but he probably was averaging as one of the NBA leaders in minutes during that stretch because the Nuggets just didn't have depth and they were banged up.

"In that stretch, he averaged 21 points and shot 45% from 3. He also averaged five rebounds and three assists. And so the question really is, is that 18-game stretch before he pulled his hamstring, is that the current Peyton Watson? Is that Peyton Watson? Four years into his career, now age 23, heading into his prime, 6-8, excellent shot blocker for a wing. Is that the Peyton Watson? Because if that's Peyton Watson, the Cavs doing a five-team trade and giving away a whole bunch of players, that's a hell of a pickup. Or is Peyton Watson the guy who he was before and after that, which is a guy who's a quality piece, a starter-quality piece, but averages, you know, 12, 13 points and has for his career shot under 40% from 3?"

McMenmamin on what the Nuggets' summer means for Jokic's future: "We know how great (Jokic) is and of course every superstar as we've seen, Brian and I in particular covering LeBron, that if you're that great, the pursuit is to try to add as much talent around you because it just opens up your window that much longer and that much wider. However, at what point do we say that they've done everything they can to field the team around [Jokic], to the point where they're in the second apron, and this could become a Milwaukee situation?"

McMenamin on what the Lakers' off-court drama means for the franchise: "The on-court product is relatively locked in. Obviously, we talked about (Jonathan) Kuminga -- who knows if that happens -- but they have 16 guys on their roster. The team's mostly going to look like what it's going to look like for next season, but when you are trying to contend and trying to add an 18th banner, you're going to have to win around the margins. And part of their intention going into this offseason was to use Mark Walter's resources and put it toward other ways that they can enhance the program. And you know Rob Pelinka stated he wanted to hire two assistant general managers. He was only able to bring in one. The other spot remains vacant on a hiring freeze. ...

"These are the type of things that while we wait for the sale to be completed with Iger and Kushner could be put on pause. And you know when you're Luka Doncic and you made the NBA Finals with the Mavericks, and now it's two straight years without getting back to that perch and wanting to have every available advantage at your fingertips to try to get back there ... When you have someone like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who's now lapped you with a championship and two league MVPs. ... We'll see how patient he's going to be with this process."

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey drafts: Which player should you take with the first pick?
stories.summary: Picking first? Here are the players you should consider with the No. 1 overall pick in fantasy hockey drafts.
stories.body:
Before mining the draft for valuable sleepers, potential overachievers and breakout candidates, first you have to grab the Shohei Ohtani, Jahmyr Gibbs, Taylor Swift, if you will, of the fantasy hockey world. The megastar to drive your team bus by reliably piling up more points on the daily than anyone else.

I can't remember another season where whittling down the list of eligible candidates to go first overall was so clear-cut. While I forced myself to make positive arguments for several other players as a necessary exercise, each member of the following quartet always emerged superior. So, in loose order, here's who to draft if you're fortunate to do so early on.

Please note that each player's strength is assessed within the framework of ESPN's standard H2H points game, in step with the following formula:

Skaters:

Goals = 2 points

Assists = 1 point

Shots and Hits = 0.1 points

Blocked shots and Special-teams points = 0.5 points

More: Sign up today | Rankings | Projections | Which league is right for you?

Nathan MacKinnon, F, Colorado Avalanche
I'll keep this short because his numbers are superlatively sweet. The Colorado center checks all relevant fantasy boxes, most with extra aplomb. Firing on net more often than anyone else for the third straight year, MacKinnon racked up 74 assists and 30 power-play points on 350 shots, while earning a sufficient number of hits and blocked shots to satisfy any demanding fantasy player. In this space last year, I suggested managers draft MacKinnon first overall and "hope he scores closer to 51 [goals] like in 2023-24." Well, he rifled home 53. Only Connor McDavid equaled MacKinnon in averaging 3.2 fantasy points per game in ESPN's standard fantasy league.

So, once more with feeling: Draft him first overall and hope he scores near 53 like last year. A total of 45 or so would also feel digestible enough.

Nikita Kucherov, F, Tampa Bay Lightning

Bit more to say here. A few weeks after securing his arguably overdue second Hart Trophy, the league's ultimate playmaker is once more ready to set the fantasy hockey world alight. No regular skater averaged more points per game (1.71) than Kucherov in 2025-26, not even that fella in Edmonton who flirted with the 140 total points mark. Exceptional terrain the elite winger might've reached himself had he not missed six games.

Never mind Kucherov doesn't fire on net as much as MacKinnon or Connor McDavid or bolster other nonscoring fantasy categories in any significant way. It's all about the production with this guy, and not just assists. In addition to providing 86 helpers this past run, he also has 44 goals to show for 76 contests. All the while delivering his fortunate managers with an average of 3.1 fantasy points/game, sharing rarefied air with only MacKinnon and McDavid in the 3.0-plus club. No reason to believe we're not in for similar numbers in 2026-27.

Plus, the 33-year-old is reliable enough nowadays. Since missing the entire 2020-21 regular season -- before, ahem, winning his second Stanley Cup a few weeks later -- then half a campaign to follow, Kucherov is serving as remarkably durable. There isn't a fantasy manager on the planet who's going to gripe about any player missing only 11 total games through four seasons. Especially when they're banging out 1.68 points/game three calendars running. Oh, and guess who's entering a contract year with the salary cap skyrocketing? Right. Even the fiercest competitors on the planet aren't immune to such extra incentivization. After MacKinnon, the Lightning star is my top fantasy pick.

Justification for selecting Kucherov first overall: His prospective power-play production. Last year's "measly" haul of 37 points with the extra skater falls well short of totals from previous seasons. Then there's the rather significant gap in quality between Tampa Bay's top unit and its second. Projecting that the elite winger sees a lot of time with the man-advantage and positively regresses back to his personal mean -- 50 power-play points through three previous campaigns -- could rationalize picking him first overall.

Macklin Celebrini, F, San Jose Sharks

It's all about the ceiling with this young man. After erupting for 45 goals and 70 assists in his second NHL season and more than holding his own at the Olympics as a teenager, Celebrini is just getting going. Growing up together with teammates Will Smith (21), Michael Misa (19) and Igor Chernyshov (20), the Ted Lindsay Award finalist is expected to take another step forward as a bigger and stronger player, equally if not bettering, his outstanding sophomore numbers. For starters, don't be surprised if he shoots more often on net, eclipsing the 300-shot mark for the first time. Proud of his 200-foot game, Celebrini could also conceivably improve on last year's total of 53 blocked shots. Those half-points add up fast.

The one fantasy concern lies in the goal-scoring department. Owning a 15.7% shooting percentage and, according to Evolving Hockey, an expected goals rate of 35 ixG, the Sharks center found the back of the net 45 times. Bit of a chasm there. Either Celebrini is just that much better, and therefore more accurate (completely plausible), or some good fortune was in play. My point is that this is why some models project Celebrini to bank approximately 40 goals -- and not 50 -- in 2026-27. Still, the lad's potential is too ripe to disregard. I'm grabbing him without hesitation, once McKinnon and Kucherov are off the board.

Justification for selecting Celebrini first overall: The Ivar Stenberg factor. Coach Ryan Warsovsky now has another option to toss alongside Celebrini at even strength and on the power play. Maybe the 2026 second overall draft pick serves as a delightful fit that brings even more out of the burgeoning superstar. If not, Warsofsky has many other talented and maturing options, even with William Eklund gone for Ottawa.

Connor McDavid, F, Edmonton Oilers

I know what you're thinking: What fantasy manager in their right mind would bypass the best player in our known universe with the second or, my goodness, third draft pick in any conventional league. I get the bewilderment, but hear me out. First of all, this teeny slide is less a knock on McDavid himself and more a reflection of the three preceding names and their dynamite potential in 2026-27.

Then there's the Oilers' power play to think about. Leading the league with a success rate of 30.6%, Edmonton's special teams unit will be hard-pressed to replicate that outstanding figure. Which means McDavid can't again count on nearing a tally of 54 points with the extra skater. Of course he makes Edmonton's unit better. Still, another 54-plus is a big ask for a player who has averaged about half a power-play point per game in his career, including the ridiculous Mario Lemieux-esque haul of 71 in 2021-22.

Another fantasy concern is the influence of the new guy behind the bench. Recognized for his commitment to greater defensive accountability and balancing lines and ice time, Mike Babcock isn't a fan of wild, open offensive play. Of course, he's still going to let McDavid cook, but more likely with the gas turned up to eight instead of 10. This is the coach both the megastar center and Leon Draisaitl wanted. While they won't give a lick about reduced personal numbers if it leads to a Cup, fantasy managers should still slightly temper their expectations.

Justification for selecting McDavid first overall: Because he's Connor McDavid, that's why. In the face of each logic-driven and exceptionally rational argument above, he could still magically score 140 points in 84 healthy games.

stories.headline: Lightning McQueen to make F1 debut at Italian GP as safety car also gets Cars makeover
stories.summary: Lightning McQueen will make an appearance at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix, with the Cars character set to take an honorary lap around Monza.
stories.body:
Lightning McQueen will make an appearance at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix, with the Cars character set to take an honorary lap around Monza.

It is 20 years since the first Cars film was released, and Formula 1 and Disney are using one of the sport's most famous races to mark the anniversary.

McQueen has arrived at Monza with a new F1-inspired design, while the Mercedes-AMG safety car used at grands prix has also been given a Cars makeover for the weekend.

The Monza plans are the latest part of F1's tie-up with Disney, which was recently extended until 2028. Cars has also been brought into the collaboration for the first time.

The collaboration initially centred on Mickey Mouse and other Disney characters and made its race-weekend debut at last year's Las Vegas Grand Prix, where Mickey appeared as part of a show at the Bellagio fountains.

It has since featured at races including the Chinese, Canadian and British grands prix.

- Monza personifies the passion that enticed Leclerc to commit his future to Ferrari

- Lando Norris announces junior racing team 'LN4 Fusion'

- Liam Lawson to drive Red Bull again at Italian GP with Isack Hadjar ruled out

McQueen, voiced by Owen Wilson, made his debut in the original 2006 film before returning in Cars 2 in 2011 and Cars 3 in 2017.

There will also be a new range of F1 and Cars merchandise available, including clothing, collectibles and die-cast models.

The Italian Grand Prix takes place from Sept. 4-6.
